name: Jussi Rahkama
headline: Turning complex operations into working systems.
supportingHeadline: I help technical service businesses build, improve and scale their operations by connecting people, processes, technology and business.
summary: I am an operations and development leader with approximately 30 years of industry experience in automotive and technical services. My career has included international manufacturer cooperation, people leadership and business development.

My career has progressed from hands-on technical work and entrepreneurship to technical training, international product support, operational management, business transformation and the development of technology-driven operations.

My core strength is understanding how complex operations work in practice, identifying the underlying causes of operational problems and building structures that enable people, processes, technology and business to work together effectively.
I am particularly motivated by environments where operations need to be established, integrated, transformed or scaled.

I believe sustainable development starts with a reliable operational foundation. Once responsibilities, processes, resources and systems are aligned, performance can be improved systematically and continuously.
My approach combines practical technical understanding, commercial awareness, people development, systems thinking and long-term customer value.
Technology is not an objective in itself. Its purpose is to solve real problems, improve reliability and enable people to perform their work effectively.

leadership.heading: Leadership creates the conditions for people to succeed.
leadership.body: People need a clear purpose, reliable operating conditions and the opportunity to improve their work.

principles.title: Purpose and direction
principles.body: People should understand what the organisation is trying to achieve, why it matters and how their work contributes.

principles.title: Build stability before optimisation
principles.body: Sustainable improvement requires a reliable foundation of people, responsibilities, processes, resources and systems.

principles.title: Strategy into everyday operations
principles.body: Translate strategic objectives into understandable actions and decisions people can apply in their work.

principles.title: Respect for people
principles.body: Give people the opportunity to contribute, learn, raise concerns and improve the way work is performed.

principles.title: Psychological safety and accountability
principles.body: Encourage people to identify problems early. Give them clear responsibilities and the support to address issues constructively.

principles.title: Root cause thinking
principles.body: Examine how the operating environment, available information, instructions, competence and resources contributed to the problem.

principles.title: Continuous improvement
principles.body: Use feedback and observations from the work to guide systematic improvement.

principles.title: Lean and Toyota Way
principles.body: My thinking is influenced by the emphasis on continuous improvement, respect for people and practical problem-solving in Lean and the Toyota Way.

principles.title: Meaningful work
principles.body: I value a clear purpose, responsible business practices and lasting improvements for customers, employees and the organisation.

principles.title: Shared openness and fair feedback
principles.body: I see openness as a shared responsibility. I aim to consider feedback constructively and fairly, regardless of who raises it. Fair treatment can call for different support in different circumstances.

principles.title: Local problem-solving with leadership support
principles.body: I prefer problems to be addressed where they are identified whenever practical. Leaders provide support and remain accountable for the operation as a whole.

principles.title: Knowledge sharing and continuity
principles.body: I aim to make critical knowledge available beyond any one individual. Sharing it supports both professional development and continuity when responsibilities change.

principles.title: Review what already works
principles.body: I review working processes as part of continuous improvement. When we decide to keep a process, we should be able to explain the reasons.

project.title: Automotive 2.0 – Rethinking Automotive Service Operations
project.subtitle: Designing an integrated operating model for sustainable, reliable and customer-focused automotive service businesses.
introduction: Automotive 2.0 explores how automotive service operations could be redesigned by examining the relationships between people, processes, technology, leadership, customer experience and financial performance.

The initiative examines the whole operating system, including how decisions in one function affect work in another. It aims to develop practical operating principles that support employees, improve service reliability and create lasting customer and business value.
The work is at the research and concept stage. Proposed workflows and system requirements are candidates for evaluation.

studies.title: Competence management and operational continuity
studies.problem: How can a service team maintain coverage of critical work as people, vehicles and skills change?
studies.context: Service continuity depends on matching jobs to available skills and keeping knowledge transferable.
studies.principles: Set role-specific criteria, involve people in assessment and protect time for learning.
studies.solution: Prototype a role-level competence map with onboarding, specialisation and coverage planning.
studies.dependencies: Agreed role criteria, accurate qualification records, training capacity and human oversight.
studies.benefits: Potential benefits include earlier visibility into coverage gaps and clearer learning priorities.
studies.risks: A map may go stale or be mistaken for a performance score. Restrict access to individual records.
studies.validation: Compare planning decisions with and without the map in realistic scenarios. Ask employees and planners whether it improves decisions and what upkeep it requires.

studies.title: Employee feedback and continuous improvement
studies.problem: How can employees raise friction in everyday work and see how it is addressed?
studies.context: Ideas and observations often arise where work happens. Some changes need a decision beyond the local team.
studies.principles: Listen fairly, address issues close to the work and explain decisions to change or retain a process.
studies.solution: Sketch a feedback loop that assigns an owner, distinguishes local fixes from escalations and closes each item with a reasoned response.
studies.dependencies: Trust, time for review, clear decision boundaries and management follow-through.
studies.benefits: Potential benefits include earlier visibility of recurring issues and stronger confidence in the feedback process.
studies.risks: An intake channel may become a backlog, expose sensitive matters or discourage participation if follow-up is inconsistent.
studies.validation: Walk through anonymised scenarios with staff and managers. Evaluate response effort, decision clarity and whether sensitive concerns have an appropriate route.

studies.title: Parts availability and operational exception management
studies.problem: How can teams identify a parts exception before it disrupts an appointment?
studies.context: An appointment can depend on part identity, delivery timing and workshop availability.
studies.principles: Confirm readiness before making commitments. Assign ownership when an exception occurs.
studies.solution: Map a parts-readiness checkpoint and an exception workflow for checking alternatives, replanning and informing the customer.
studies.dependencies: Reliable supplier information, parts identification, appointment ownership and timely status updates.
studies.benefits: Potential benefits include fewer avoidable interruptions and earlier customer communication.
studies.risks: Availability data may be stale. Premature alerts can create unnecessary work and substitutions need technical review.
studies.validation: Use representative scenarios for delays, incorrect parts and uncertain availability. Compare decision timing and rework with the current process.

studies.title: Workshop capacity and resource planning
studies.problem: How can a workshop make credible commitments when jobs differ in duration, equipment and required skills?
studies.context: Effective capacity depends on technicians, bays, tools, competence and uncertainty in incoming work.
studies.principles: Plan against real constraints, allow for variation and define how priorities can change.
studies.solution: Explore a capacity view that matches work to critical resources and supports replanning when conditions change.
studies.dependencies: Usable job estimates, resource availability, competence coverage and agreed priority rules.
studies.benefits: Potential benefits include more reliable appointment promises and less last-minute replanning.
studies.risks: Detailed planning can consume more time than it saves. Optimistic estimates may hide bottlenecks.
studies.validation: Use representative schedules to test disruptions and resource conflicts. Assess planning effort, feasibility and effects on commitments.

studies.title: Customer communication and shared operational information
studies.problem: How can different service roles give the customer a coherent update as work progresses?
studies.context: Preparation, workshop work, parts and handover generate information at different points in the service relationship.
studies.principles: Record decisions where work happens, assign update ownership and only share information relevant to each role.
studies.solution: Prototype a shared view of the service commitment, status, next action and communication history.
studies.dependencies: Accurate source information, role-based access, agreed terminology and clear customer communication responsibilities.
studies.benefits: Potential benefits include fewer repeated enquiries and more timely, consistent updates.
studies.risks: Duplicate entry or excessive notifications could increase administration. Customer data needs appropriate access controls.
studies.validation: Review realistic service scenarios with staff. Compare the effort to record and retrieve updates and check whether each role has appropriate access.

studies.title: Operational performance and balanced KPIs
studies.problem: How can leaders assess service performance without improving one measure at the expense of customer commitments or quality?
studies.context: Capacity, productivity, inventory, margin and service reliability influence one another.
studies.principles: Use clearly defined indicators with context and review both outcomes and trade-offs.
studies.solution: Sketch a balanced review that connects availability, delivery reliability, quality, workload and commercial performance.
studies.dependencies: Consistent data definitions, reliable inputs and a shared understanding of decisions each indicator supports.
studies.benefits: Potential benefits include clearer discussion of trade-offs and earlier detection of local optimisation.
studies.risks: Poor definitions, delayed data or targets used without context can distort decisions.
studies.validation: Test whether sample indicators explain realistic cases, reveal trade-offs and justify collection effort. Establish baselines before considering targets.

capabilities.title: Understand
capabilities.body: See how complex operations work in practice, identify dependencies and recognise the root causes of performance problems.

capabilities.title: Build

capabilities.title: Transform
capabilities.body: Improve performance by aligning people, responsibilities, processes, technology and commercial objectives.

capabilities.body: Build reliable operations and develop them through continuous improvement, competence development and long-term customer value.

operatingModel.title: How I approach operational development
operatingModel.body: My approach has developed through operational transformation, technical services, business integration, team development and the establishment of new operations. It starts with understanding the real work before changing the system.

steps.title: Understand the operation
steps.body: Observe how work happens and how people, processes, systems, customers, resources and financial performance interact.

steps.title: Identify the root cause
steps.body: Distinguish symptoms from underlying problems. Examine working conditions and available support before drawing conclusions about individual competence.

steps.title: Clarify the structure
steps.body: Establish clear objectives, responsibilities, priorities and ownership.

steps.title: Connect the missing elements
steps.body: Develop connections between people, information, systems, processes and organisational functions.

steps.title: Translate strategy into action
steps.body: Define how work will happen, including workflows, decisions and exception management.

steps.title: Engage people
steps.body: Involve employees, listen to concerns, provide support and follow through on problems raised.

steps.title: Measure, improve and scale
steps.body: Establish a stable foundation, monitor performance, learn from results and improve systematically.

insight.title: Building reliability throughout the customer lifecycle
insight.body: Technical service and aftersales are part of the customer relationship from before the initial purchase through the life of the vehicle or product.

sections.title: Maintain and restore operational capability
sections.body: Technical service helps customers operate reliably and restores capability efficiently when failures or disruptions occur. Reliability, availability, delivery performance and trust all contribute to customer value.

sections.title: Design for reliable delivery
sections.body: Identify quality and delivery deviations early, assign ownership for risks and corrective actions, and plan capacity. Use intuitive systems, clear communication, constructive supplier and partner cooperation, and long-term competence development to support a commercially sustainable operating model.

sections.title: Evaluate the effect of technology on work
sections.body: When assessing a system feature, I ask what work it removes, what work it introduces and whether it improves the overall operation.
